utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, we are Thursday, the 8th of May, 2008. I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, the witness and Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us in the courtroom or outside the courtroom. Before resuming the cross-examination, I would like to move into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-002, yesterday, at the beginning of the cross-examination, I asked you whether, in me, personally, or in the Serb Radical Party, you saw any danger due to which you sought protective measures, and your answer was in the negative; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now I would like to know the following. When was it that you found out for the first time that you were supposed to appear as a Prosecution witness here in the courtroom in the trial against me? When were you first told about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, the first time this was mentioned to me as a possibility, now, I don't know exactly, two or three years ago, when I was here last time. I think it's been five or six months now that I've been officially asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were told by the Prosecution twice that you were planned to testify in this trial. The first time, they referred to it as a possibility, and the second time, they notified you officially that you would be a witness for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the third time, when you came to The Hague for proofing; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I understood that not as proofing, but I knew that I would be a witness when I came to The Hague then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During these three contacts with the Prosecution, did you express any fear to the representatives of the OTP, to the effect that you felt endangered by me or members of the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you sure you never said any such thing to them? I'm not going to torture you any longer. Your answer was, "No." This is not a trap question for you. This is something that I have to put before the Trial Chamber now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- rather, Judges, last year, when you got a request -- a joint request from the Prosecution for protective measures, you received an addendum as well, explaining the reasons for which protective measures were sought for each and every witness. As for this witness, VS-002, the explanation said at the very end, so I'm not going to talk about the content of the planned testimony. It says: "Witness VS-002 lives in a territory that is easily accessible to the followers of the accused." So to me, to me, this is what I'm adding now: "The witness is afraid he will be exposed to intimidation and revenge if the public finds out that he testified, and the Prosecution shares this fear. The testimony of this witness in connection with the participation of volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, the Serb Chetnik Movement --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. It might not be perhaps prudent to stay in open session. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. First of all, Mr. Dutertre, from time to time you complain that Mr. Seselj speaks too fast and interrupts the witnesses, and now you interrupted. I didn't even have the end of the translation of what Mr. Seselj was saying. So I did not hear what you said. Could you please tell me what you said again?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Your Honour, questions relating to protective measures are being evoked here, and I think that maybe it would be more prudent to go back into closed session and to redact what was said these last minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall consult my fellow Judges first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I say something before you decide, if I have the right to do that before you decide? Afterwards, it's too late. I think that there is absolutely no specific reason to move into closed session, because in this paragraph that I'm reading out, there is no reference to any name, fact. Nothing is mentioned except for fear that I or the Serb Radical Party could threaten the witness. Please let me read out those two sentences. There's absolutely nothing that should be read out in closed session. I can guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Dutertre, what would you like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is a motion -- it is a motion that was filed confidentially, under seal, so nobody can read something that was under seal unless the Trial Chamber had lifted the confidentiality. So I object that excerpts from documents that were filed under seal be read in this trial. Your microphone is open, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber has deliberated on this and decides the following: The sentence that was read by Mr. Seselj may remain in the domain of the open session. This sentence talks about general matters relating to reasons linked with protective measures, so this cannot identify the witness at all. Secondly, the Trial Chamber wishes to mention to Mr. Seselj that if he continues to read excerpts from a confidential motion, the Trial Chamber may adopt a different position if the read passages mention elements that may identify the witness directly or indirectly. Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being very careful, Mr. President, and I think that so far I haven't done anything that could jeopardise the identity of protected witnesses, although in some cases I fervently wanted to do that. But in the case of this witness, I really never wanted to. You have seen the kind of witnesses who appeared here, so you can understand what I'm saying. Let me just read these two sentences, and I guarantee in advance that there will be nothing that would be subject to measures of secrecy. Subsequently, you can declare this secret if I make a mistake, but I'm sure I won't make a mistake. So now let me read it out from the beginning, because I was interrupted halfway, in half sentence, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, for the record, the Prosecution objects to the accused reading out, in public, a filing that was filed confidentially. That, in our submission, is improper, regardless of the contents that might be contained within what he says. If we file something confidentially, then the office has taken a position that the material should not be in the public domain, and as a result of that the accused should not be allowed to read into the record material that was filed confidentially. As a matter of principle, Your Honours, we think that's wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you are a prosecutor with a great deal of experience. You know very well the Trial Chambers have the right to lift the confidentiality of any document filed confidentially. Even more, Trial Chambers have the possibility to render confidential ex parte documents public. So you are right, it's at our own discretion. When it comes to confidential documents, you must remember that Trial Chambers have the right to lift the confidentiality - it's at our own discretion - when there are no -- when there is no need to maintain the confidentiality of a certain document. So I would like to say, for myself, I do not know what the position of my fellow Judges are, but according to me, justice must be done clearly, without any confidentiality, justice must be transparent, except of course for documents that regard either the personal safety of a witness, or of a victim, or when it contains state security matters. But for the time being, the sentence that was read does not jeopardise absolutely anybody's position and does not violate any rights. And as the accused said himself, if the Trial Chamber deems that we can redact certain elements, we will redact. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Certainly, the Prosecution has no quarrel with the notion that the Chamber can lift the confidentiality or the nature of a filing that was made ex parte and confidentially. What our concerns are go to the broader issue concerning witness protection. When we meet with witnesses and they request protective measures, they are generally informed that such requests will be made confidentially. If we then move into a situation where the public becomes aware that in the future, notwithstanding the fact that a motion was made confidentially, that the accused can come in and divulge parts of that, that will have a devastating affect on our ability to bring witnesses in here who might need protective measures. Rather than allowing the accused to read this into the record with the proviso that it can be subsequently redacted, we would suggest it would be better to go into closed or private session, and if the material can then be put into the public domain, so be it. But we're dealing with a situation where, in our respectful views, Your Honours, utmost caution must be taken when we're dealing with protective measures concerning witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, Mr. Mundis, you are proposing that we first move into private session. Mr. Seselj would then read those excerpts, and the Trial Chamber, if it deems there is no problem, may at that point say that it can be read into open session. Is that what you're proposing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So let me confer with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In order to find an acceptable compromise that would satisfy all parties, we shall first move into private session. Mr. Seselj will then read the two sentences in question, and the Trial Chamber will decide on what will ensue, and I may, myself, reread those two sentences at a later stage in order for it to become public. So, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to read out in public as well these two sentences from the Prosecution's explanation why protective measures were sought for this witness, because I believe that in this way, I am not challenging the witness's testimony, or his credibility, or anything that has to do with him personally. In this way, I'm just branding the procedure applied by the Prosecution, because I'm saying -- it says here: "Witness VS-002 lives in a territory that is easily accessible to followers of the accused. The witness is afraid that he will be exposed to intimidation and revenge if the public finds out that he testified, and the Prosecution shares this fear. The testimony of this witness in relation to the participation of the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, the Serb Chetnik Movement, in the massacre on the farm of Ovcara is of crucial importance for the Prosecution case. The testimony of Witness VS-002 will probably cause fury among many members and sympathizers of the Serb Radical Party and Serb Radical Movement. Many of them, like those that Witness VS-002 will mention, might try to take revenge upon him or his family if they find out that he testified."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we did not have the text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few times in front of you here, the witness said, decidedly, yesterday and today, several times that he never felt any danger coming from me, personally, or the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber would like to add this so that it's on the transcript: The Trial Chamber has authorised you to read a confidential document pertaining to the protective measures after having considered the opinions of the Prosecution and the witness on this matter. This is why the Trial Chamber has entitled Mr. Seselj to read out this excerpt of the document. You may proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-002, I listened to your entire examination-in-chief, and I read your statement from 11 years ago, and I read the transcript from your hearing from last week. I never found a name anywhere of any volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party who, according to your testimony, participated in the Ovcara crime. You now -- are you now able to recall any name of any man that you know for sure was a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party and that he had taken part in this crime? Please, can you try to remember very well if you are able to find any name at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I was not able to remember then, in 1997, I'm definitely not able to remember anything now, after 10 years, so the answer is that I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. VS-002.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This other thing that I would now like to read briefly probably is also affected by these protective measures, so I'm letting you know in advance. And this is going to take a minute or two at the most, so perhaps we can then move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we'll adopt the same procedure. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-002, in your previous testimony, the first time you testified - I don't have to mention the case, it's not so important - and this is on page 1174 of the transcript, you said that there were all sorts of volunteers in Vukovar and all sorts -- and reservists. This indicates that not all volunteers can be described as volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The cockade that you received from me, after I actually took it from a person, from my escort, that was Petar Panic who was my personal escort for several years and my escort at the time, did you see an identical cockade like that on anyone in Vukovar? So what is the sense of my question? Was that cockade unique in the way it looked in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe so. Look, I didn't see such a cockade on others, but I don't believe that it was created specially for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't made for anything concrete. This was sold on Belgrade's Main Street. I mean, everybody knows the manufacturer. But what I'm asking you is: Did you see one like that on anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you couldn't say in any way that that cockade was a marking of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, definitely not. It's possible that some radicals there also wore a cockade like that, but I didn't see them all wearing it uniformly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, all right. You said that there were reservists there from different groups. Some were from Novi Sad, some were from Crnojevac. You even mentioned some Nis Rangers, but you said that you didn't know what kind of a formation that was. In any event, all of those groups of reservists, volunteers, soldiers, they were all part of the JNA; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, you mentioned that there were some individuals who were walking around Vukovar. "From what I can recollect, they could have been armed, but they didn't belong to anyone." Do you recall saying anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there were persons like that; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And their motives were of a criminal nature; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm terribly sorry to interrupt, but the pace is very fast, the interpretation is done from Serbian to English and from English to French. When the witness answered, since the pace was so fast, I only heard then the interpretation into French. I cannot make any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, you speak the same language I do, and I'm under the impression that the interpreter in the French booth is interpreting directly from Serbian into French, meaning that we are following as the original goes on simultaneously. So maybe you get a delay on your end of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it's the same thing, but the witness is answering so quickly that I cannot make any objections. I would kindly ask the pace to be slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please try to slow down, and especially when you want to emphasise a very important event, do so. And this is what I do: When I wish to emphasise an important sentence or something very important, I slow down intentionally so that people pay attention. So if you want to highlight something, such as the cockade that you mentioned earlier, slow down, and you will see that automatically people will pay more attention to what you're saying. These are various techniques. You know them better than I, of course, in terms of speech techniques.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-002, I am constantly being criticised in this courtroom, but what can I do? I have to bear all of that. Don't be surprised because of that. I would like you to tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, some critiques can be constructive critiques.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... I can when somebody's younger and they can be corrected, but I'm incorrigible, Your Honour. They have declared me as incorrigible a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to tell me everything you know about Spasoje Petkovic, called Stuka, without mentioning your own relations with him so that you could be recognised? What did you know? What did he do during the war in Vukovar? I'm keeping in mind what you have already mentioned in your statement, so now if you could give us the whole picture about him. But avoid saying anything that would take us into private session. I would like this to be said in public.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stuka, if I can put it in general terms -- it was rumoured that Stuka was very dangerous and that he liked to kill, so that -- well, the reason for that was that while he was a regular soldier, he was personally connected to another friend of his, a soldier. He was seriously wounded in the spine and became an invalid. So I think that he wanted to seek revenge for what happened to his friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know any specific instances of Stuka killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned some events in my statement, but I never saw the killings directly, myself. But it's logical, you see, because quite simply I didn't like being present when things like that were going on, so I avoided situations like that as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And was Stuka at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Stuka kill at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took people out of the hangar, and he didn't bring them back. And as far as I learnt, they were killed with a Scorpio rifle -- Scorpio gun, he had this gun for liquidation purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that pathological analysis found that there was some 18 weapons used to kill the prisoners at Ovcara? The press wrote about this. I think there were 18. There was just one Heckler among them. Did you say he had a Heckler or a Scorpion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Scorpion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was just one Scorpion among all those other weapons; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Bozo Latinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Or Boro Latinovic. What's his real name? What's the correct name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the surname Latinovic. I could describe the man. Now, as far as -- I think it was Bozo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And was his nickname "Krajisnik"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then it's Boro Latinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Boro Latinovic, nicknamed "Krajisnik." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was he at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Now why did I ask you that? Because both of them were accused by the court in Belgrade, and then they struck a bargain with the prosecution, and the indictment was withdrawn if they agreed to give false testimony against other accused. Very well. Now, yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to intervene for something else, but, yes, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, once again I think we should omit talking about false testimonies, whether it's relating to this witness who is here or a witness who's testified in other matters. I think it's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not want to intervene for that, and it was brought up by my colleague yesterday, and the Trial Chamber would invite once again, Mr. Seselj, unless he really knew that in Belgrade it was withdrawn because there were some false witnesses, but then that has to be proved, but I did not want to intervene for this. I wanted to say something else. Many weeks ago, I requested the Prosecution -- and now I'm talking to Mr. Mundis officially. The Trial Chamber requested the Prosecutor to hand us a copy of the indictment regarding a case that was judged in Belgrade, and we still haven't received it. The Trial Chamber requested it, but I did not get it yet, and I am very surprised, because the Trial Chamber made that request, the Prosecutor could have called the prosecutor in Belgrade to ask him to send him, by fax, the indictment in Serbian. That should have been given to the Translation Section immediately. So it would be incredibly ridiculous that I ask the accused to get this document. So, Mr. Mundis, how is it so that when witnesses come and we talk about Vukovar and we talk about the Belgrade trial, how is it so that we don't have in our hands the indictment from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the CLSS is working on the translation of a number of indictments from the former Yugoslavia for transmission to the Chamber. We attempted to file those earlier. They were rejected on the grounds that we didn't have the translations yet. So we're working on the translations, and they will be provided as soon as they are ready and available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But this indictment has a priority. It has to be translated as soon as possible. It is a priority. Some witnesses come to talk to us about Vukovar, and there were trials with people who are being tried right now or who will be tried, and we have to be able to check some data, and we do not have the indictment to do so. I will stop here. Let's continue. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to draw your attention, Mr. President, to the fact that the first-instance judgement in the Belgrade trial was appealed, fell on appeal by the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court ordered a new trial, which is underway, so that the qualifications that I gave you a moment ago are not far from the truth. In fact, they're very close to the truth. Now, I have before me part of the transcripts from the trial in Belgrade, and I provided the service yesterday for it to be copied for the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution has it, because the Prosecution disclosed it to me sometime ago. But I selected just some excerpts from that -- or those transcripts which contain the statement of some of the accused. So what was in open, public session. There is no secret testimony, so there's no reason for us to go into private session, either, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-002, you said in examination-in-chief that Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni, you did not see him at Ovcara; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, I have to inform you now that for a brief time he was, indeed, at Ovcara, but for a very short period of time, and I assume that you weren't there at that time. So I have before me here the statements given by Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, one moment, please. The Prosecutor wishes to say something. He is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Your Honour, I myself put the question to the witness as far as if he saw Kameni. He did not say that he didn't see him, he said that he didn't remember seeing him. So if the witness is to be quoted, I would like him to be quoted precisely, or maybe one should quote a transcript page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj asked you if you had seen Kameni. You saw Kameni or you don't remember seeing him? It's not exactly the same thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be true to say that I don't remember seeing him. But how can I say, here and now, that I didn't see him? Well, I don't remember having seen him. So -- well, I'm doing my best to answer the questions truthfully, to the best of my knowledge, so this places me in a very stupid situation, whether I don't remember seeing him -- well, I don't remember seeing him now. Whether I did see him, what can I say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a very important question, and if Mr. Seselj puts that question to you, it's because it's important for him. But it's also important for the justice, for us -- for justice or for us. Was Mr. Kameni in Ovcara? You could say, if you know, yes, you saw him in Ovcara, or if you do not remember, you can also say that you don't remember. But give us exactly the right answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to make. I just informed the witness that Kameni was at Ovcara for a brief period of time. The witness says he doesn't remember seeing him, so if he doesn't remember seeing him, it's the same as saying he didn't see him. "I don't remember seeing him," that means he wasn't there. That's so clear to me that I have nothing further to ask. But I'm informing him of this now so that I can continue with my questions, because I have collected the transcripts here of the interviews by Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni, Predrag Milojevic, Kinez, and Marko Ljuboja, nicknamed Mare, what they said in the court in Belgrade. So now on the basis of parts of those transcripts, I'd like to ask the witness specific questions. It's not my aim to force him to remember at all costs something that he didn't see, but what is interesting for me is part of the statements given in Belgrade, and then I'd like to hear his comments, the witness's comments and testimony to those portions of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. We all agree on this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I provided you with those transcripts. I'm on page 10 now of the transcript which begins with "06260125." That's the number. And then it goes on to "0143," page 19 of that set. Kameni says that the Staff of his unit was in Nova Ulica Street, and you said in your testimony that it was in his house. He says that it was in Vaso Robija and his brother Pero's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that change anything substantially? Is that nearby or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's possible. I assumed it was Kameni's house. I really didn't know where Kameni lives, either before the war or after the war. So what I meant was, yes, Nova Ulica, that's where -- I thought it was Kameni's house. Possibly it's not his. The possibility is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know at that time that on that day when I was in Vukovar, I spent the night there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know you stayed there for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I remember that they took me to Kameni's house to spend the night. So it wasn't the house in which the headquarters were located, but another house in the vicinity. That's what that means. Well, it's not important. Now, do you remember that that same night, right next to the house where I spent the night, an aeroplane -- an agricultural plane belonging to the Croatian Air Force dropped a load of explosives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that it happened then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the next day, Tomislav Peternek, a famous Serbian photographer, took a picture of me in front of that house, stripped to the waist, washing myself, with a volunteer pouring water for me. Do you remember that picture, that photograph? "Nin" published it and some other magazines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the photograph, but I do remember the journalist who was with my unit for 10 or 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tomislav Peternek was a very brave man. He went to the frontlines and took photographs of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was armed with a camera, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. 002, we've been told to slow down, but I think it applies to you, rather than me. Would you pause before you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On that same page, Kameni refers to Major Tesic, Major Borivoje Tesic. That's who he is. I assume you knew him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 1st Assault Battalion, right, or rather the 1st Assault Detachment? He was the commander of the battalion within the Guards Brigade, and then he was appointed commander of the Assault Detachment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he commanded the battalion, as far as the Guards Brigade is concerned, under whom the Territorial Defence left flank belonged to. Now, the exact names of the units which he commanded, I don't know. I don't know the exact names of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you spoke about the structure of the units of the Territorial Defence here, I noticed, and with the help of Kameni's statement, I'd like to ask you additional questions on that same subject. Kameni says they were all under the command of Borivoje Tesic, that in the evening they held meetings, and that coincides with your statement, that they coordinated operations. And Kameni goes on to say that the battalion that was commanded by Major Tesic had three companies. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I assume that that is correct, that what Kameni said is correct, because he knew the top echelons better. I was a soldier, he was a commander. I know about Tesic because I happened to see him two or three times, and I know that Tesic knows of me, of my existence, so -- now, I never had to go to him to report or anything like that, so I really didn't know all the officers and who was in command of what.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, on the next page there, Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni, goes on to explain who the commanders of the three companies were, and he says -- and that's paragraph 1 on page 20 -- that they were Captains Radic, Zirovic, and Bojkovski. And then he goes on to say: "Captain Radic was along our axis of activity, where Miroljub and myself were, Miroljub and I," and so that was the Petrova Gora Detachment, and Miroljub Vujovic was its commander. And then there was the Leva Supoderica Detachment whose commander was Kameni, and there was the company of Captain Radic as well. Now, what is Kameni explaining here? He's explaining that each JNA company was linked to a Territorial Defence detachment and they worked in unison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably that is correct, theoretically speaking. However, in our particular case, that is to say, in the case of the unit that I was in under Miroljub's command, the only assistance we had from the army was by way of ammunition and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We're talking about action here. Do you understand me? Your unit is going into action and Captain Radic's unit is going into action. That's the Guards company. And then you have the Leva Supoderica, belonging to Kameni?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. Then he goes on to say Captain Bojkovski went with a unit under the command of Stanko Vujanovic, and Captain Zirovic, to all intents and purposes, had lagged behind and that he found it difficult to advance because his unit was rather inert. That's what Milan Lancuzanin says here in his statement. Do you agree that what -- how he describes it is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as Bojkovski is concerned, I really can't say. Now with respect to Captain Zirovic what I can say is that it wasn't his fault that they were inert, because he only had two or three soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've already said that the commander of the Vukovar Territorial Defence was Jaksic. However, Jaksic did not have a single unit immediately under his command and did not take part in the fighting. He was in the rear all the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down for the benefit of one and all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: ... there were two or three units, one under the command of Stanko Vujanovic, Miroljub Vujovic, and a third unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're going way too fast. Follow the transcript. You will see that the interpreters are shouting for help.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll speak much more slowly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Anyway, Kameni is testifying here and says there were a total of three units, one under the command of Vujovic, one under the command of Stanko Vujanovic, and one under his own command. Now, at the bottom of that same page -- or rather he says somewhere there that it was Jaksic's intention for Kameni's unit to be the 3rd Company of the Territorial Defence, in actual fact, whereas he was placed under the direct command of the Guards Brigade already. And the Prosecution in the Slobodan Milosevic trial, while I was a Defence witness there, the Prosecution showed me a document signed by Milan Mrksic, where it states that all the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party should go to the Leva Supoderica Detachment. Is this something new, are you hearing something new now or did you know about it at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: What they did and where they sent whom and who was under whose command, I really wasn't much interested in any of that. Well, I don't know whether it was a power struggle as to who would be the commander or whatever, but I didn't like it then either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, there was some competition and rivalry among the three of them for supremacy; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So although they cooperated in battle, on a human level there was rivalry and competition; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, here on page 29, Kameni is previously speaking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Kameni is explaining how he came to be at Ovcara. He said he heard something was going on there, and he says that he drove in in a Passat car. Did you see that Passat car of his in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness said that he didn't remember, and I know that this question should not be put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But maybe he saw a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in that case, there's an assumption, the assumption that Kameni had a Passat. So in his question, there's a hypothesis put to the witness, so I object to that sort of question. First of all, we should establish whether Kameni had a car, what kind of car he had, and if he drove in a car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, in order to avoid that the Prosecutor puts objections, which of course makes us all waste time, try to put questions to the witness in such a way so that the Prosecutor is not rising to put objections.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever questions I come to ask, I can assure you, Judges, that the Prosecutor will jump to his feet all the time, because he's dissatisfied with these proceedings, the way the witness is testifying, the results of the cross-examination, and I am not able to help him out there. But this is what I want to ask the witness: Kameni is explaining that he arrived at Ovcara, and you have that in paper there, and that with him were Kinez, Ceca and Marko Ljuboja, and when he saw that the prisoners were there, they were in the hangar, he tried to take out some of those prisoners, and he gives names. And I want to ask this witness whether he knows the names of those Croats whom Kameni wanted to take away from Ovcara, because they were friends of his. That's what I want to ask, but how am I to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Kameni, on page -- and I'm jumping over this now, going further -- on page 33, says that he wanted to take away Jarabek -- well, he enumerates them, so I don't want to run the risk of making mistakes, let's take it this way: Jarabek, Sarek, Medjasi and Zvonimir Caleta. Did you know these Croats from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just think I know Medjasi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, this Zvonimir Caleta person, he says he was the maitre d' at the Hotel Dunav [as interpreted], and that he was related to his friend Mile Belanovic. So he says, I wanted to take him away and take him to that relative of his. Did you know this maitre d' at the Danube Hotel? If not, we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then Kameni goes on to say that seven or eight of them -- that he did separate -- select seven or eight of them and that he wanted to take them away from Ovcara, but that the people who were there, that those who were there told him that they would get up on to the trailer-truck and that he could follow the trailer-truck. Does this ring a bell? Does the situation seem familiar, that certain people were set aside, not to mention names, that they wanted to set aside people to save them, whereas they were taken in quite a another direction and killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So something similar happened to Kameni. And Kameni goes on to explain now, and I have here, on the following pages, where he says that he set out in this Passat car of his, following the trailer-truck, and that suddenly the trailer-truck took a turn off the asphalt road and went into the fields, and that he was surprised to see that, and that he kept following the trailer-truck and got stuck in the mud off the road, and that the trailer-truck went further on and he was no longer able to catch up with them. So was that the usual method, that trailer-trucks set out along the asphalt with the prisoners and that after a certain amount of time and distance they turned off into the fields?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, I don't know what you're about to say, but the question is an important one, as far as I'm concerned. Now, we are cross-referencing what the witness has been telling us and what Kameni has been saying about the trailer-truck. Why do you want to raise an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Kameni says in a trial where he is an accused is his business. Anybody can put the question he likes. But that is not why I'm on my feet. I believe the witness has never been to the site of the execution, if I understand this correctly, so he can't say anything about it. He can only speculate the way in which the trailer-truck might have been able to go -- be driven around the field and get stuck in the mud. So he can't answer this in any way, and this is why I have risen to my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Kameni now explains here that he returned very angry and that he quarrelled with the people who were in charge of this dirty job at Ovcara. Then an incident took place. They started insulting him, saying that he's a coward, and in a derogatory sense they used a vulgar term relating to female genitals, and with Kinez, Ceca and Marko Ljuboja, he left Ovcara. That is it in the briefest possible terms, the content of his statement. You did not hear of anyone being insulted there, these derogatory terms being used, as far as Serbs are concerned? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. My colleague has just brought this to my attention. This legal document you are reading, which is Kameni's testimony during the trial, is this a statement which is part of the trial that has been cancelled or is this a testimony that followed the opening up of the trial again, when the trial resumed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a statement during the first trial, and the date here is the 29th of June, 2004. That is what is written here, and this was submitted to me by the OTP, the OTP of The Hague Tribunal. They probably thought that they would scare me when they provided me with this pile of material, and I sit leafing through that for nights, and then they regret ever having sent such things to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, all right. The Trial Chamber will assess the value of this document, but for the time being, since the trial has been cancelled, we are starting anew. Since the trial has been cancelled, everything prior to that has been cancelled also. So in legal terms, without wasting any time on this, theoretically the document you are reading does not exist. So for your information, it would be interesting for us to know Mr. Kameni's version of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all these documents exist, in legal terms, but there is no judgement only. These documents were taken over by the new proceedings and a single sentence suffices, if an accused person says, "I fully subscribe to the statement I made personally." Believe me, I know that, because I was tried there for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you are well-versed in the proceedings here, so you are providing additional information to some of the questions of my colleague. You have just told us that this document was tendered in the new trial, so we have acknowledged this and note what you are telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In relation to Kameni's statement, I just want to put one more question to the witness. Kameni states here that already on the 18th of November, people were leaving, being disengaged from his unit, and that Leva Supoderica was reduced to about 30 members in total. Did you see that from the 18th of October, onwards, many buses were taking territorials and volunteers and reservists from Vukovar, taking them back to where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see them being driven away or not, but I wasn't even interested in that. I know that people believed that the war was over, and I myself had the opportunity to ask for a leave to go to Novi Sad, and that would have been approved. My problem was that I did not have any transportation. At that time, I hadn't passed my driver's exam, either, so I didn't ask for leave at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's what he says. I thought that you knew something about that. You don't, so I'm not going to insist on it any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I'm going to stress this, because this is extremely important, and it's very important for the following reason: You were there. We know that the tragic events that occurred in Ovcara took place on the 20th. Now, what we are interested in is to know, after, I'm using a general term, the Serb forces took Vukovar, without going into any detail, you were there, did you have the feeling that a lot of the fighters then left after Vukovar was taken? They went of their own free will or they went because they had been given orders, or did you feel that everybody was waiting for potential orders? You said yourself that you wanted to leave because it was over, but it was a problem. What I'm interested in is the fate of all the others. How did you understand the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, as far as I can remember now, the army issued permits for departures, about 200 per day. I cannot remember exactly now. I know that there were one-time permits and also multiple-use permits. So you could get permission to leave on a particular day, that you could leave the zone on a particular day. I personally needed a permit that would be valid for seven days or for a month, because after receiving this permit, I would need a day or two to find transportation to Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When the Bench is running the proceedings, that is a different approach. Now, you have just told us about something which we've never heard about before. You've just told us that you remember after -- seemingly after the fall of Vukovar, the army gave -- on page 35553 [as interpreted], they gave orders to let soldiers go on leave. Are you quite sure? Page 55, page 55. Could you answer my question, please? You said 200 soldiers were authorised to go on leave per day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not say that. I said that the army could issue 200 permits per day, and that I heard that, which is not to say 200 soldiers. So 200 soldiers could have received these permits, but perhaps they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the permit could have been a collective one, one permit for several soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that that is the case, but, really -- I mean, really, I do not remember. I know that permits were being issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For instance if an entire bus is leaving, a single permit was sufficient, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you. I have Marko Ljuboja's statement here. Did you know him? Mare was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Look, if I'd see his picture, I'd recognise him for sure, because the name rings a bell. I don't have his face before my eyes now. I cannot say that I directly know the person, but if I were to see his picture, I'd certainly recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Never mind. Marko Ljuboja was briefly at Ovcara with Kameni, and what happened in Belgrade was that Kameni was convicted and Marko Ljuboja was set free, because they wanted to link Kameni up to me. But now we're getting to Predrag Milojevic's statement. His nickname was Kinez. I don't think there's anything else of interest except that his story corroborates Kameni's story. Oh, yes, another thing regarding Marko Ljuboja's statement, he mentions this Topola, who you mentioned as well. And he says that Topola was in the Leva Supoderica unit, but that Kameni expelled him from the unit because of a lack of discipline or perhaps cruel treatment, or something like that. Could that jog your memory, because you could not say where Topola was? You saw him at Ovcara, but you didn't know what unit. After Topola was expelled from Leva Supoderica, was he in any other unit or was he roaming Vukovar on his own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me, it was news that he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are several questions wrapped in one, so perhaps we could focus only on what is essential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please focus on your question. Make sure that we understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will be as specific as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We had Goran Stoparic's testimony here, who also stated that Topola was expelled from the unit. Now we have Marko Ljuboja's statement who says the same thing. I'm just asking the witness whether after that, Topola belonged to any unit or whether he moved about Vukovar on his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. You can put your question again, but I would like to put a question to Mr. Mundis. The document which relates to Kinez -- Kameni's testimony, during the trial in Belgrade Mr. Seselj said these documents were given to him by the Prosecution, and it is my colleague who's drawn my attention on this. Now, if you had disclosed them to Mr. Seselj, you have a translation of these documents into English. I don't see how you could be sending documents to the accused without having read them beforehand. Mr. Mundis, do we have a translation into English of these documents, and if you do, the Trial Chamber would like to have these documents. The.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If the reference, Your Honour, is to the indictment concerning the Vukovar case in Belgrade, that is 65 ter number 2775. The other documents I will make inquiries with respect to and get those in the hands of the Trial Chamber if you don't have them already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's this document that Mr. Seselj is talking about [indicates]. The number is 0626-012. So this is an official document. There is a seal on this document, and this is a document that Mr. Seselj received. So you must have translated it into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my knowledge, there's no translation into English of this document. The documents in B/C/S are very great in number, and to date I have not received a translation of this document. It was disclosed to the accused, and it is certainly relevant in terms of Rule 66(b). I have just received a two- to three-page summary yesterday which the Trial Chamber might be interested in, but I have no more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Seselj. Put your question again. I interrupted you. I am sorry. Please put your question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to observe, first of all, that I am convinced that had the OTP had this translated into English, they probably wouldn't have sent this to me either, because this is a treasure box for me for data. However, in 2005, they did seize some documents from me, because they said that they mistakenly submitted them to me, and they never told me what the mistakes were. They searched my cell, then they took out what mattered to them and they returned the rest. To this day, I don't know what it was that they took from me then. But what can I do? That is my fate here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-002, I just asked you whether Topola, at the time when you saw him in Vukovar, was alone, a lone individual, or whether he seemed to belong to some unit, or whether somebody else was moving about with him. What is your impression about that? I assume that you saw Topola in Vukovar even before Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, I may have seen him before that, but I don't remember him in particular. I only remember him from Ovcara, and it didn't seem to me at all that he was a member of this unit, of the radicals, because I would have had that impression to this day, had that been the case. I immediately categorised him as a volunteer independent of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me just say one thing. It wasn't only volunteers of the Serb Radical Party on -- in that unit. I'll tell you what Kinez says here. If the OTP would be so kind as to find that first video footage where Topola was identified and then the photograph where another Prosecution witness identified Topola, and if we could show both photographs to the witness. Well, I'm not counting on that extent of kindness from them, and also this other group of Chetniks with Chetnik flags marching through Vukovar, and one of them only has a Chetnik hat. If you don't want to, I'm not going to insist. Perhaps I'm counting on too much kindness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, without relying on the courtesy of the Prosecution, the document you are talking about has been shown to the Trial Chamber, and it has a number. So you're perfectly entitled to ask the Trial Chamber to display it on the screen, since it has been tendered into evidence, because you want to show it to the witness. I don't have a number, but if you give me the number, it's not a problem. I just ask the Registrar to display the document in question on the screen, and then he can say, yes, it's Topola, or it's not Topola. Unfortunately, I didn't know that you were going to address this issue. Otherwise, we could have given instructions to look for the document. But, unfortunately, I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to admit sincerely that it just occurred to me to mention this. I didn't really prepare for that, and I didn't ask for the number, and I didn't ask the Registry to help me. It just occurred to me right now that this could have been useful. But since this is now not possible, I'm going to move on, because I cannot count on the kindness of the Prosecution. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. That you don't rely on the courtesy of the Prosecution, that's one thing, but you can rely on the Chamber's eagerness to do everything that can be done to make sure that all the evidence is adduced, particularly in the presence of a witness. Now, a document has been tendered into evidence. This document relates to Mr. Topola. Was Topola in Ovcara or not? This could be an important question, particularly in light of the case you have just made, and you said that Topola had been thrown out of the unit and that he was an individual on his own. Now, if the witness says this is Topola or it isn't Topola, it could be important. I would like the Registrar to find this document. Perhaps we can lay our hands on a photograph that has already been admitted. If I remember correctly, this photograph had been shown to a witness, and the issue concerned Topola. Normally speaking, if the Registrar goes through the list of exhibits, we'll be able to find it again. Otherwise, we won't. Mr. Seselj, this is what I wanted to say. If the Prosecution doesn't want to make our life easy or be -- very well, but the Trial Chamber, if the exhibit has already been admitted, can find it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to mention the kindness or not of the Prosecution. I've noticed that oftentimes the Prosecution has provided the accused with a series of documents, so I don't think that they're not willing to do this. And I don't understand why the Prosecution should remember the number of the video clip if you yourself don't remember it. We don't remember all these numbers, the Registrar not either. So why should the Prosecution have to remember the number? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think clearly the Prosecution is under no obligation to assist Mr. Seselj when he is cross-examining a witness. He is in charge then. Of course, we can't remember all the numbers of an exhibit -- all the exhibit numbers. Of course, I shall look for it and address it during the redirect, and I shall try to find the number. So we are willing and in any case working in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like the Registrar to give us a countdown, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you've had one hour and 20 minutes. You had three hours and five minutes, so you have -- let me subtract.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can help, an hour and 20 minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have 105 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One hour and 45 minutes. I mentioned, because it had occurred to me -- I really didn't prepare. I can withdraw all that if the Prosecution is unable to help me. You recall that we had a video still of a big soldier with white cross-belts and somebody lying on the ground, and then we had Witness 007, I think, who identified another person as Topola. This first person was identified as Topola as well, so I would like this witness to look at the video footage and the photograph and to tell us if either of these two people is Topola. I wanted -- actually, this footage was shown in the courtroom several times, and it was separate from the testimony, when there was a group of soldiers marching, wearing JNA helmets, with a Chetnik flag in front of them, and among them, in the middle, is a person with a Chetnik hat and a cockade. Well, if this is not possible, I will withdraw it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But now I would like to ask the witness if he knew Predrag Milojevic, called Kinez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know who that person is. I spoke with him on two or three occasions during the war in Vukovar, but I don't really know him all that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was Kameni's deputy, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess so. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you must have noticed that throughout the whole war he wore a five -- a red star on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was very strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it was not only Chetniks who were members of the Leva Supoderica unit; that's one proof?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot exactly remember his explanation, but I asked him once why he was wearing the red star. There was an explanation that he gave, but I can't remember what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that he was never a member of the Serbian Radical Party, nor was sent to the front as a volunteer of that party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't want to say anything or distance myself from him. He's a very good man and an honest fighter. But it's important that you confirm for me that he wore this red star, a communist symbol.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the second -- in the second set of papers, on page 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The numbers were too fast for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: ... he says at the top of the page that in the Leva Supoderica Detachment, the number of people went up to 400 even. Is this something strange to you? Was there such a high number of members of that detachment at any given point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't reply to that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to press you on that. He also came with Kameni, according to his statement here, to Ovcara, where they remained briefly. In the circumstances, actually, he explains that in the same way as Kameni, Marko Ljuboja and Ceca. Did you know Ceca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had heard of him and I probably did see him, but I would need to see a photo to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, then. It's not important. This is what he said in his testimony before the Belgrade court, I'm thinking of Kinez, he describes what he saw at Ovcara. So when I read that to you, it's a short passage, I would like your comment: "There was a mass of people there. You could see that something was not going well. The last thing that a person could think --" Yes, I will read more slowly. I am being warned to read more slowly: "You could see that something was not quite right, but the last thing that a person could think of was the fact that there were many soldiers there. There were active-duty soldiers. This was about 5.00 or 6.00. There were soldiers there. There were senior officers there, officers. Military policemen were there with cross-belts. These were guys with bulletproof vests, professional bulletproof vests, so these are not volunteers, these are not people from outside. "And I could never think, when the loading was going on, because at the time it was normal to carry out transfers of prisoners. At that time, this was something normal, to load them up. I don't know where they were being boarded to go where. There were stories that they were going to Mitrovica, here or there. So it was quite normal for them to be boarded, but nobody would ever think that soldiers were there or that anything like that would happen. Who would think of anything like that? "To this day, it is unclear to me that such a failure occurred and exactly what happened. If there is God, we will find out what happened here, and there is a god." Do you believe that this is the way in which many soldiers thought at the time who happened to be there at that time? I'm talking about regular soldiers, TO members, reservists, volunteers, that nobody could even conceive that these prisoners of war would be liquidated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally think that in the beginning, nobody assumed or thought that they would all be killed. I personally assumed that they would be interrogated, that perhaps they would be beaten to find out some truth or not, but it didn't even occur to me that they would all be killed. So this testimony of Kina and the only thing that I cannot agree with is -- and that is that I did not see any soldiers with white cross-belts. But, look, because I didn't see them, it's possible that they happened to be there at a point in time when I wasn't there, because I said that I wasn't there longer than an hour or an hour and a half. But, in essence, I think I answered your question. No one, practically until -- well, how shall I put it? Nobody assumed that anything that happened would happen until it was actually starting to happen, until it was actually happening, so it's possible that somebody from the Command knew something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The soldiers with white cross-belts, do you mean that those were soldiers of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, the soldier with the white cross-belts, and not only in the Guards Brigade but in all the former JNA units, there was a military policeman. This is a little bit strange to me, because I would have definitely seen such soldiers, had they been there. I say again I was not there on a couple of occasions. I would be -- I was away for an hour or two at a time, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now I'm on page 14 again. I am skipping over many parts of the statement. Predrag Milojevic confirmed that the unit was reduced to 40 people, he said. And we saw that Kameni said that it was down to 30 men. Probably they cannot be exactly identical in their information after so many years, but he said: "I think that there were about 40 people, that there were not more than that, because, look, with the fall of Vukovar, all the fighters that had been at the front for a long time, the first thing they wanted was to go home. Since General Mrksic was in The Hague when we were making the plan for the action, I was personally present at that meeting. He said, "The end is nigh," he said that personally to me, "We have many men." And then he said, "Let's remove these people gradually," and this is what we were doing so that practically when the 19th came, we only had about 40 people. On the 18th, perhaps there were a bit more." Does anything seem strange to you here when he says that he received an order from Colonel Mrksic to start quickly reducing the number of men in the units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The witness stated earlier that he didn't have many contacts with the SRS unit. I do not see what he can answer, and I would like to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do not see what is the relevancy of that question, but I, as a judge, do see a relevance as to what this person, Predrag, said in Belgrade. You may continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how tall Kinez was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was taller than me, perhaps 1 metre 90. He was some 10 centimetres taller than I was, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But in any case, he's considered to be a tall man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, look, this is interesting, what he says here in his testimony; that General Vasiljevic, who gave a statement in The Hague, he testified in the Milosevic case in public session and one part of the testimony was in closed session, and I still haven't received that, unfortunately, he said that he edited a serial truth in Vukovar which was published in some Serbian newspapers, "Ekspres Politika" or something, and he that mentioned Kinez. In describing Kinez, he said that he was an exceptionally small, short man, and I'm saying this because when I was arrested at the end of the Sablja action, he was arrested after the assassination of Djindjic, and this was called the Sablja action, the sabre action, when almost 20.000 people were arrested by the Serbian regime; you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that when I was taken in at the end of Sablj a, when the people in Belgrade who were working on shedding light on this case, first they came and told me to report to Belgrade at 3.00, and I reported there. As soon as I entered, there was a Mr. Milosevic there, he's thinking of some policeman whose last name is that, and then Vasovic. As soon as I entered, one of them said, 'Sit,' and so I sat down. They told me three times, "Stand up.' First of all, why should I stand up? They asked me, 'Is there another Kinez?' They asked me how tall I am. I would stand up. They asked me, 'Is there another Kinez?' I said as far as I can remember at that time I couldn't remember -- there wasn't another Kinez in my unit. They asked me how tall I am. I said that I was 188 metres tall, in my boots I'm 1.91 metres." This is on page 18, Your Honours: "I sat down. We began to talk about Ovcara, about all of that. When I made my statement, they asked would I be able to dare to take a lie detector test. I said, 'Why wouldn't I dare?' Then they refused that." And then the President of the Trial Chamber interrupted him and said: "Well, let's not discuss that." And that it's very characteristic that he was interrupted at that particular point in time. Then he wanted to explain: "I went and took the lie detector test there. I was questioned twice. Then I was taken back again and they asked me again, 'You must recall that there was another Kinez.' I said, 'I don't know.' Mr. Vasovic then told me that he had information that there were seven men with the 'Kinez' nickname. Seven men with the same nickname of Kinez," and so on and so forth. He's simply telling a true anecdote here, how General Vasiljevic said that Kinez was an exceptionally short man, the police came to arrest him and Kinez is there 1.90 centimetres [as interpreted] tall? Is this a surprise to you, that somebody is describing Predrag Milojevic, called Kinez as a person who was exceptionally short?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know -- I know that the Kinez that we're talking about is 1.9 metres tall. This is the one that I know. I don't know of any Kinez who is short. If you're thinking of any Serb with the nickname Kinez, then I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As far as I know, there's no person who had the nickname of Kinez except Predrag Milojevic. I never heard of such a person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, neither did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Witness VS-002, I would like to put several questions to you which I believe you will probably insist you answer in private session, so I'm just letting the Trial Chamber know this in advance. I wouldn't wish in any way to -- well, before that, I would actually like to put some other questions, before we move to closed session, if you permit me. I just failed to ask you one thing. I've just remembered it. It's indisputable that a serious crime occurred at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in this crime, a certain number of people took part. We don't know exactly how many of them, but a certain number of people did participate in that. Among them, mostly the inhabitants of Vukovar were recognised. There were some others as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You agree with that. Before the serious crime occurred, there was cruel treatment, a lot of hate was expressed. Tell me, you knew some of those people who participated in that, who generated this hatred. Did many of them have private reasons to express such hatred; that, for example, Croat soldiers, Ustashas in Vukovar, killed one of theirs, burned their house, robbed them or anything like that? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. If Mr. Seselj wishes to evoke some names, he should first establish whether the accused knows them and what he knows of what these people had in mind. This question is general, it is vague. It calls for speculation. One has to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please try to rephrase these questions. Just take the witness to the example and then ask him questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll talk about his personal example in private session, because he was a victim of the war in Vukovar as well. I know that, and I have reliable data to that effect. But let me ask him in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does he know that the Croatian authorities, the police, the paramilitary formations, and among them the ZNG, so-called, the National Guards Corps and other formations, that in the Vukovar Municipality area, before the Guards Brigade arrived, that they had killed about 150 Serb civilians? Do you know that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was killing. I never knew the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you confirm that there was large-scale killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. People were taken away, and they never returned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Now we could move into private session to protect the witness's identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you try playing the video, and if that's not it, then we're not going to dwell on it any longer.
