utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not the video clip, obviously. I asked for a group of soldiers marching, and in front of them is a Chetnik flag, and in the middle, among the soldiers with helmets, there is a man with a hat. But never mind. Since the OTP hasn't found this, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-002, do you know anything about the political situation in the area of the Vukovar Municipality in the beginning of 1991? This was after the elections in Croatia, when the HDZ reinforced their power.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, I was not in Vukovar at that moment, but I know that the situation changed drastically, because I spent a weekend or two there. All of a sudden, Serbian and Croatian cafes appeared separately, so it was suggested to me that I be careful about where I go out. And this was said to me several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know where Trpinjska Cesta is in Borovo Naselje, I assume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know of the meeting of the HDZ at Trpinjska Cesta in February 1991, that was called by Tomislav Mercep and was attended by Vladimir Seks, Ivan Vekic, and Branimir Glavas from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the HDZ had celebrations and that they had meetings and rallies in villages, and that they roast meat. But I don't know about that particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that they made a decision to cleanse Vukovar of Serbs? First of all, that all Serbs be removed from political and other positions, that Serb citizens be intimidated in order to move out, and if all of that fails, then to start with physical liquidations? Do you know that that was the decision made by the HDZ at that meeting of theirs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Look, I don't know about that meeting, but sometime around then -- well, before the war, on television there was that programme about the arrest of that general of theirs, Djuro Decak. When the intelligence people recorded him with Spegelj, what should be done to the Serb people, that's what they were discussing, the Serb leaders, that they were all supposed to be removed, killed, things along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that already towards the end of 1990, the massive arming of members of the HDZ started, that automatic rifles and ammunition were distributed to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that their volunteer units and paramilitary formations were reviewed, and that this review was attended by 2.000 people in February of 1991 in Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know, just tell me briefly that you don't know. Do you know of the large-scale operation of removing all ethnic Serbs from Borovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I assume you've heard of Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of his crimes against the Serb civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that he brutally openly committed crimes to such an extent that the Croatian authorities started minding and Marin Vidic Bili asked the authorities from Zagreb to have him replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard something along those lines, but later after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that he caused a big massacre of Serbs in Pakracka Poljana and Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Blago Zadro was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was some general of theirs from Trpinjska Cesta, if I'm not mistaken. I cannot guarantee anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A general from Trpinjska Cesta, so he was one of their paramilitary leaders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear him speak openly about all the Serbs who do not accept the Croatian Constitution having to leave Borovo Naselje one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was a large Serbian population in Borovo Naselje; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear of the Serb Zdravko Egic, the director-general of Borovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who was replaced only on account of the fact that he was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Look, I wasn't in Vukovar in 1991, practically, not until September, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Marin Vidic Bili is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was the deputy mayor in the municipality, and then after Dokmanovic was told to go away, he took all power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that he replaced all the Serb cadre in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that he personally replaced Dr. Rade Popovic from his position as the administrator of the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know that he personally replaced him, but I knew that Rade Petrovic [as interpreted] was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that all Serb police officers were dismissed from the Vukovar police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the reserve police forces were augmented by admitting many Croatian civilians, including notorious criminals armed with the latest weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that armed incidents were provoked in order to intimidate these Serbs in Vukovar villages?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the names of all the villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't object to the question, but there are a series of questions that are put to the witness. We don't know what time-frame they relate to, the attacks on villages. When exactly did all this happen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please clarify this. Please ask -- please specify and ask whether this happened before the Serbs entered Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we clarified. We clarified that all of this is happening before the armed conflict between the Guards Brigade and the Croat rebels. All of this preceded the war. This is the year 1991, and everything is happening before the actual war, before the JNA got involved in the conflict at all. We started from February 1991. We haven't even reached the summer yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that, Mr. Seselj, but the public at large might not be aware of this. Some people might have questions about it, so please try and be accurate. You list some of the events that took place, but you could perhaps just sum it up in one sentence and ask the question which you are undoubtedly going to have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I promised that I'm going to cut this short. I'm constantly putting questions and that I'm going to cut short my cross-examination, so all I want is "yes" or "no." I'm going very fast, so let's not waste time, so that I don't change my mind about my previous promise that I will finish at 1.00. I'm not using almost a full hour of the time that I had allotted. So the Prosecutor is doing this on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about the mining of Serbian catering and other facilities in the area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Belgrade newspapers were systematically seized when they arrived in Vukovar so that it would not be sold at the newspaper stand, so that the Serbs could not read the Serbian press?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, you don't know about that. Do you know that news stands that carried Serbian press were mined, or bombed, or blown up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about a major police action in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that before that, an accord was reached to go for a favourable solution of the problem, to lift the Serbian blockades -- barricades around the village and to restore normal life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know about that, but you know that Borovo Selo was a majority Serbian settlement, almost 90 per cent was Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croat police officers were defeated there, and there were a large number of victims there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm only asking you this because I'm especially proud of this victory, but I'm not -- it doesn't matter if you don't know it. Do you know who Marin and Ivan Pliso are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Marin Pliso. The other name is not known to me. Marin Pliso had a reputation -- or it was said about him that he had imported weapons, Kalashnikovs from Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that together with Ivica Franjic, Draca Mrkobasic, Josip Gazo, the Mulnar brothers, Joza Horvat, Josip Mazar, and Ivica Kasalo and others inflicted terror against the Serbian population in the Vukovar Municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, you're aware of that. Very well. Do you know that a large unit of the Vukovar police administration was engaged in the action of harassing Serb citizens in Borovo Naselje on the 4th of July, 1991, and that Zeljko Marusic, Zoran Gotal, Ante Roso and Blago Zadro were in command of that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about the marking of Serb houses, clearly -- clear markings of Serb houses in order to frighten the Serbs who lived in them and to incite Croat extremists to harass and rob the Serbs who lived there and to perpetrate violence against them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that these people organised illegal entry-and-search actions of Serb houses, sporadic arbitrary fire, that they harassed them mentally and physically, that they robbed Serbian property, illegally deprived them of their freedom, and killed Serb citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Dragan Mijatovic, called Macak, and Stojan Stojanovic from Borovo Naselje were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that a large number of citizens of Serb ethnicity were killed and that their bodies were thrown into the Danube?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that, but I can't say that I know about it for sure. I did hear of it, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear when Serbs began to flee from Borovo Naselje en masse to Borovo Selo, that in the cornfields between those two settlements, the Croat paramilitaries and police officers killed a number of Serbs, and that the corpses of those Serbs remained in the cornfield, and that a stench was spreading from these corpses, causing additional fear among the Serbs? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear of any of these Serbs, Blagojevic, [indiscernible], Uros Tomic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vorkapic is known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that without any reason they were searched, beaten and taken to the Osijek prison and that no legal documents were issued against them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard something, but this was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about the mining of Serb houses, them being blown up and demolished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the houses of Serb Uros Tomic, Jovica Brdenic [phoen], Svetko Tomic, Marko Milivojevic, Jovan Tintor, Bajo Blagojevic, Mico Vorkapic, Mileta Skeledzija [phoen] and others were blown up and demolished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that, specifically. Probably this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know any of the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You don't know those people, but you did hear of it, about this blowing up and looting of houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about the Borovo Naselje areas called Budzak and Kriva Bara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about those areas of that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in July 1991, a pogrom was carried out against the -- of the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know, I'm not going to -- do you know that Kapel [phoen] Milica and Golub Marceta were killed, Andja Akif, and these were elderly and weak people, [indiscernible] and Bozo Lukic's wife, and "N. Lukic," unknown, I don't know her first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Look, I really don't know what was happening there, especially not in Borovo. I know roughly what was going on there, that Serbs were harassed, but I don't know any incidents by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of Luzac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a large pogrom committed there of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there were problems there, that the Serbs there had problems, but I don't really know exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the commander of that pogrom action was Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Ivica Franjic Srna was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Then we're going to move to Dalmatinska Street, which is more familiar to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Josip Tomasic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that all houses on Dalmatinska Street were searched, robbed, that Serbs were detained, taken to the police administration where they were beaten and some of them were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Look, I wasn't in Vukovar until the end of September 1991, so I'm not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I'm not insisting on anything that you don't know. Feel free to tell me if you know or you don't know. These are -- this is information of mine that can be used in the cross-examination of any witness, and none of that can be disputed. I'm just seeing if you know any of this or not. Did you hear of Serbs called Nedeljko Turukalo, Petar Turukovic [phoen], Cedo Latinovic, Jovo Dragosavac, Petar Zoric, his wife, Lazar Ristic, Drago Grujic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard of many of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that they were all killed in Vukovar's Dalmatinska Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if this happened in Dalmatinska Street, but I do know that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. I mean it's not "very well." It's a sad matter. I'm just using that as an expression. Did you ever heard of Drazen Gazo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that Serb restaurants and shops were demolished in Vukovar, itself; for example, the Migros shop owned by Branko Sucevic; the Restaurant Grmes, also owned by Branko Sucevic; Restaurant Royal, owned by Bozo Sucevic; Restaurant Maci Raj, owned by Zivko Strika; Restaurant Veselj Bosanci, owned by Djordje Pavlovic, and then that passenger vehicles were blown up, the car of Vlado Tepavac, for example, that Branko Sucevic was killed, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know of those restaurants, I know that they were blown up, but I didn't know who the owners were by name. I know just that they were Serb owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The JNA investigative organs established that this was committed by Drazen Gazo, that's why I asked if you knew about him. This happened in June/July 1991. Did you hear of Zdravko Komsic, Stejpan Mackovic and Ivan Mikulic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know that in the village of Sremski Cakovci, they opened fire at the restaurants owned by Serbs there on the 29th of June, 1991? And then in Sotin they killed Mihalj Nadj and Joco Ivkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They killed Mihalj Nadj by mistake, thinking that he was an ethnic Serb, but he was actually an ethnic Hungarian. Did you hear of Franjo Bracko [phoen], called Brada?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that Marin Vidic is from Lovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know him before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You heard about that crime. A lot was written about this in the press, about the Serbs committing the killing of Croat citizens in the village of Lovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that, but I don't know any specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that this was preceded by a Croat crime, when 33 ethnic Serbs were killed in that same village of Lovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did hear about that, but I heard it from others. I heard talk, but I don't know anything specific about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croatian authorities, in late August 1991, in order to attack a JNA barracks, sent to Vukovar from Zagreb Mile Dedakovic, who was previously a JNA officer, his nickname was Jastreb, as well as Branko Borkovic, called Mladi Jastreb, who was also a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they were members of the defence in Vukovar during the war, but I don't know when they were sent to Vukovar from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that they formed four ZNG battalions with Marin Vidic in Vukovar; one was in Borovo Naselje, one was in Mitnica, one in Lusac and Sajmiste, and one was not linked to any particular part of town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't even interested in that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear of Ferdinand Lukic, called Jeja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me remind you, he's an international criminal, smuggler of stolen cars abroad and in the area of the former SFRY, there was a search warrant issued for him by international police forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I try not to socialise with criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's nice, but sometimes criminals take the main word in society, and then we are faced to deal with them, aren't we? Have you heard of legionaire Anto Roso?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about the castle of Count Eltz in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is a protected cultural monument, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the legionaires of Ante Roso then occupied that entire castle. Do you know that there were some legionaires in Count Eltz's castle during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps that some Croatian paramilitary soldiers used some anti-hail or hail-breaking instruments and used them to fire against the Vukovar citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Did you know that in 1991, pursuant to orders of Marin Vidic and Bojkovic, an ZNG military police formation was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that they even had military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, this is the first time that I'm hearing this now. I'm not interested. I wasn't interested in all the things on the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm not insisting on this. What you know, you can confirm. What you don't know, you can just say so and everything will be fine. I just want to cover as many details as possible and to see what you know and what you don't know. If you don't know, it's not a problem. Somebody else will know. Do you know that on the 3rd of September, the barracks of the JNA in Vukovar were blockaded pursuant to Marin Vidic's order, and he was a special emissary of the Croatian government, and the electricity, the water and the telephone lines to the barracks were cut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how this was blockaded, but I know that the blockade was imposed because after that the army lifted the blockade sometime in late September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that immediately after the blockade, since you don't know any details of the blockade, the barracks was fired at from all sides, from all available weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that after the barracks was blockaded, the Serbs suffered the most; they were arrested for no reason, they were spent -- they were put into prison, they were tortured, harassed, many of them were taken to the Danube where they were killed, that some of them were killed in the yard of the kindergarten, on the street, in shelters, and so on and forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You say know about that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that not even to this day is it known what happened to some of the Vukovar Serbs and that there are quite a number like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are listed as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the captured members of the JNA were killed straight away, even if some of them were wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you ever -- did you hear of the fact that a JNA member's head was cut off, that there was an incident like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what about the killing by flames from a Brena [phoen] that were used by some Croatian guardsmen to kill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, let's move on. Do you know that the military courts of the JNA, immediately after the liberation of Vukovar, brought criminal proceedings to bear against members of the Croatian paramilitary formations, members of the ZNG, National Guards Corps, the police and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. I'm not sure whether they were military courts, but I do know that certain lawsuits were instigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear about Tomas [indiscernible]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were commanders, the commanders of some paramilitary units, and accused of crimes committed in Dalmatinska Street. You haven't heard about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Seselj, if you really want a name to be taken down in the transcript, say it very slowly. Otherwise, it has absolutely no use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-002, do you know who Zdenko Novak is, nickname Miner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't hear of him mining Serb houses around Vukovar and placing mines in Serb settlements so that the civilians would be affected, without any military need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know about the mining of some Serbian settlements to cause casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have here quite a lot of information about Croats from Vukovar against whom legal proceedings were taken before the military court, but do you know what happened to all of them afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milan Panic freed them all and had them exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that with the first plane, the greatest Croatian criminals from Vukovar, including Vesna Bosanac and Marin Vidic Bili, that General Aleksandar Vasiljevic went to Zagreb personally with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you learned something along the way. Mr. VS-002, that completes my cross-examination, unless the Prosecution can offer up some videotapes or photographs, if they've found them subsequently, or perhaps the Registrar, if you have anything at your disposal, but I don't want to go into detail about the Croatian criminals from Vukovar because the witness confirmed a large number of crimes that took place. He confirmed that. And as we're dealing with crimes that are indisputed and which cannot be wiped out by anything now, I have no reason to tire him with any more details. Can you tell me if you have managed to find some material that could be presented now in the form of photographs, tapes and so on? Nothing, right. Tell me, please, just one more thing, a few details?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said, during the examination-in-chief, that you considered the cockade to be a symbol of affiliation to the Chetnik movement. Did you mean the Serbian Chetnik Movement, which existed as a section within the frameworks of the Serbian Radical Party, or did you mean in general terms the Chetnik movement as an abstract concept, of an undefined concept, but rallying people of the same political and ideological ilk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I considered that no political party can appropriate the Serbian Chetnik Movement as being its own. Every Serb nationalist has the right, in case of war, to be a Chetnik. That's my vision of things. And I also consider that the Chetniks were -- are a military, not a political organisation. I think that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, if they're organised, they can be an organisation of war veterans as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Or they can be the descendants of the one-time Chetniks, such as the people from the -- the fighters from the Salonika front and things like that, their descendants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So we can't limit that to soldiers, can we? It can apply to various categories of civilians; would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, categories of civilians, if they were Chetniks or if they have any links to Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Even if it is a freedom-loving idea that guides them; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I can agree with you fully on that score.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. In order to allow the Prosecution to have their time, and not to have to come back here from afar, thank you, VS-002. I cannot appraise and evaluate your testimony in total, because I don't know about many of the things that you spoke about, but I think that your testimony was very honourable, especially with respect to those parts of your statement that can relate to the indictment against me, and I wish to state that publicly. You really did testify honorably in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With regard to redirect, Mr. Dutertre, you have 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I will try to be quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, page 6080 and 6066 of the transcript, in answering a question put by the accused, you said that up until the last moment, the various members of the volunteers and members of the TO present on the field did not know what was going to happen with the prisoners. On page 6547 of the transcript, I was trying to understand. Why did you help Perkan and Berghofer, and I asked you what you thought that would happen to them, and you said -- you knew very well at that point, didn't you, that they were going to be executed, and this is why you took them out from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get where.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I think that this is an unbelievable example of manipulation with witness testimony. We should differentiate between what the witness's opinion was, looking at it from this point in time. When he says, "I don't think they would be alive today," and what he thought at the time when he quite simply wanted to take these people away to a safe place, to avoid them being mistreated, and I don't think this manipulation should be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No manipulation whatsoever. I only quoted the words of the witness. And maybe it's something he may have thought later. And my question was very clear, that is, the question that I have here before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You knew very well at that time, didn't you, that Perkan and Berghofer would be executed if you didn't take them out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this. Look, my father told me to help if I was able to Berghofer or Perkan, so when I saw them at Ovcara, I did my best to help them. At the time, I could not have even assumed that all those who had been captured there would be killed. But when you help someone, you try and help him so as to avoid that that person be mistreated. So, quite simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm only intervening because I wish to save time, and also it's in the interests of justice. The interests of justice supersedes the interests of the parties. In answering a question put by the Prosecutor, you said that you helped Perkan and Berghofer. What we would like to know is the following: When you helped them, what kind of help did you do? Is it because you knew them and you helped them, or in your mind you thought that something horrible would happen and you wanted to make sure that they would not be executed, and you wanted to do everything in order to take them out of the hangar. Do you see the difference here? You can say many years after, "This is what I thought would happen," but what we would really like to know is to find out at the time, on that particular day, at that very moment, what was in your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, at that point in time, well, it was the first time that during the war there was mass killing taking place. So before that, it couldn't have even entered my head that anything like that could happen. I couldn't imagine anything like that. Quite simply, I was saving them from being mistreated. It never occurred to me that they would be killed. Had somebody asked me before, "What do you think is going to happen," I would say, "Probably they'll be interrogated, perhaps somebody might die during that questioning," but I didn't think they'd all be killed, personally. And if that was to be done that it was going to be done by the military court, because when the army comes in, they have the right to court-martial, so as villains, and that was the law in the SFRY, there were rebels against the regular state, they would be court-martialed, and this would be done in a legal way. They would accuse him for treachery against the state, high treason, and then that would have been the result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: On page 6066 of the transcript, you said that Mr. Miroljub Vujovic maybe knew as a commander, but not other people who were there knew about it, and you also said there was a lot of coming and going, and you yourself were gone on two occasions, and according to you, for several hours. Given all this movement, you were not able to know, given that all the people from the Serbian side were present in Ovcara, you were not able to know what they knew of what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: On page 6572 of the transcript, you mentioned that the official announcement of the massacres in Ovcara was made rather late in the day. This official information, I think, needs to be clarified. On page 6573 of the transcript, as regards the group of people which you separated from the hangar when you got back from Velepromet, who boarded a tractor, you said that you had the premonition -- you had a premonition. You felt that something ominous was going to happen, but that you couldn't imagine that they would be executed. And prior to that, 6548, lines 13 to 15, you said that you had understood that Miroljub Vujovic had used you to separate the prisoners on his behalf, so that these could be executed. This is how things happened. It is then that you understood, when you separated the prisoners, that they were going to be executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I understood only when I separated the second group. When I separated the first group, I went back inside, and it was only when I took out the second group that a light flashed and I realised what was happening. And then I went to talk to Miroljub and asked him whether there was the possibility of me not doing that anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Therefore, you asked him to stop doing that, because you had clearly understood that the fate of these people was to be executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing I didn't know was whether there was the possibility of somebody with more authority appearing and putting a stop to this, with greater authority than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Let me now move on to the visit, Mr. Seselj's visit to Vukovar. On page 6608 of the transcript, the accused put questions to you. He wanted to know when he visited Vukovar, whether it was possible to gather an assembly in order to deliver a speech given the security situation and the artillery fire. You answered by saying that it was not possible at that time. When you later went to Kameni's -- Stanko Vujanovic's house, when you received the cockade --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor does not have the right to put things that way. The witness said that that was in [indiscernible], and he mustn't mix that with Vujanovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I didn't remember. That had escaped me, and I thank him for having specified this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you were in Kameni's house, were there any security problems, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "security problems".

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Was there any artillery fire at that time, still, any sniper fire? What do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there wasn't any problem in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 6608, you say that you had not heard of a speech or a gathering of soldiers to hear a speech delivered by Mr. Seselj. You said that you'd heard about someone who was -- someone whom you knew well. In light of what had happened to this person who was fairly close to you, you were not concerned about anything else, you weren't interested in being made aware of the fact that Mr. Seselj had addressed an assembly of people, because your state of mind was such that you weren't really interested in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: At the time, I really wasn't interested in any political matters, precisely because all that had happened, so that -- that I was under stress, that's true, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And when you say because of what happened to you, you mean what had happened to this person who was close to you; is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know whether the 80th Motorised Brigade of Kragujevac, was in Vukovar during the conflict in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, whether that was exactly the 80th Motorised Brigade, but they were people from Kragujevac, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecutor is expanding the re-examination. The 80th Kragujevac Motorised Brigade wasn't brought up either in chief or in the cross-examination. I don't mind that it's mentioned but I have to reprimand the Prosecutor and tell him to stick to the rules. We talked about that in some other instances, and so I am raising the objection for reasons of principle, that the brigade wasn't mentioned either in chief or during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now on the basis of the cross-examination, what entitles you to discuss this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the chain of command and the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness 002, do you know the name and the rank of the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know who Colonel Milorad Vojnovic is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is impermissible, because this gives me the right to cross-examine with respect to any new matters that the Prosecutor raises in redirect, and how am I going to have time now to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please allow me to say that I disagree with you for the following reason: You, yourself, during your cross-examination, you highlighted the possible presence of the colonel who had been ordered to go to Ovcara. He had received instructions from a general. Perhaps the Prosecution does not like your version of the story. In that case, the Prosecution, by putting a question during in redirect, he is entitled to discuss this, and this colonel in question could be the person who was part of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Why wouldn't he be entitled to ask a question, like you were allowed, and afterwards you can call your witness to put -- witnesses to put questions about this colonel. But the Prosecution may think that this is the same colonel and not your colonel. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: On page 6660 of the transcript, you were questioned at length about the presence of a colonel and a captain of the JNA in Ovcara, and according to your testimony, you said that you thought the second person was a captain. And then you were asked whether you had seen these two colonels before, and you said, "No." So this is my question: You heard someone call this person "Colonel," and another person whose rank you cannot identify, and you believe the second person was a captain, but it certainly wasn't two colonels you saw on that same day, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last point, Your Honour, just very briefly. I'd like to address the issue of artillery and the way the town was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You said, Witness 002, that the town could have been taken in one day, and that the artillery kept on shelling the town, sometimes preventing you from moving forward. Were you trained in any way in the use of artillery fire during combat operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't understand the question. What training do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you attend a training course or anything of that kind on how to use artillery fire when a town is being taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Obviously, the Prosecutor is trying to provoke the witness, because not even Theunens, the Prosecution expert witness, could say that. He didn't know the difference between an automatic rifle and a submachine gun. So this has no sense. In the cross-examination, we talked about what the soldiers said, what their comments were about this artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you did your military service in the JNA, the witness did his military service in the JNA, so the question that could be of interest to all of us is: When you do your military service, are you trained in any way in the use of artillery weapons? He will say, "Yes," "No," "I don't know." The second question: When he was seconded to this unit in Vukovar, did he receive any kind of training on how to use artillery weapons; yes, no, we don't know. This is a purely technical matter. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the witness, on page 100, line 1, that he had received no training. And just one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Were you present when the orders -- when the orders to use artillery weapons were given to the artillery unit, and did you attend the officers' meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before adjourning today, I would like to clarify something in light of the request you made this morning, but I would like to address this in private session. This is not going to take -- this is not going to be long. Registrar, can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, very well. We are back in open session. Today's hearing has just ended. I would like to thank, on my behalf and on behalf of my colleagues, the witness coming here and testifying, but I believe that Mr. Mundis wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I did, if I could before we adjourn, concerning next week, in the event the witness scheduled for whatever reason is not available. We do have two backup witnesses available for next week, but I again would ask that we go into private session, perhaps that this witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's lower the blinds, and in future please raise these housekeeping matters at the beginning of the hearing and not at the end of the hearing, so that we do not go overboard. Let's move into a private session right now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're back into open session. Today's hearing is adjourned. We will resume next Tuesday, and the hearing will take place in the afternoon. So the hearing will take place at 2.15 next Tuesday. Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of May, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.20 p.m.,
